title: Why Cheetahs Quit After 20 Seconds 🐆
description:
Why does a cheetah, the fastest land animal at about 100 km/h, give up a chase after roughly 20 seconds? It isn't overheating: a 2013 study that put sensors on six hunting cheetahs found their body temperature barely changed during the sprint, so the real limit is how fast that springy, all-out gallop burns energy.

Sources:
https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/its-a-myth-that-cheetahs-overheat-while-hunting
https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/cheetah
https://doi.org/10.1098/rsbl.2013.0472

topic: The Cheetah Paradox: why can the fastest land animal only sprint for about 20 seconds?
script: A cheetah quits after twenty seconds, and you'd never guess why. It hits about a hundred kilometers an hour, zero to seventy-two in two and a half seconds. Each stride covers seven meters, four strides every second. Its spine bends like a spring, its lungs and heart are huge, and its tail steers like a rudder. People thought it stopped because it overheated. But in 2013, scientists put sensors on six cheetahs. During the chase, body heat barely changed. It only jumped after a catch, probably from stress, with lions nearby. So what stops them? That springy sprint burns energy crazy fast, so a full sprint lasts about twenty seconds, just a few hundred meters. Miss by then, and the cheetah's done. Only about half its chases end in a meal. Would you rather be that fast for twenty seconds, or slower all day?
key_facts: Top speed about 100 km/h (National Geographic); Smithsonian gives 96-112 km/h
0 to 72 km/h in about 2.5 s; stride about 7 m at about 4 strides per second (Smithsonian National Zoo)
Flexible spine works as a spring; large nostrils, lungs and heart; tail acts as a rudder (Smithsonian)
Full sprints last about 20 s, a few hundred meters (Smithsonian ~274 m; NatGeo 'a few hundred metres')

Hetem et al. 2013 (Biology Letters): sensors on six cheetahs; temperature barely changed during hunts; rose 1.3 C in 40 min after a kill vs 0.5 C after a miss, likely stress; overheating idea called a myth
About half of chases succeed (Smithsonian; NatGeo says ~40%)
Premise fixed: sheet row said heat buildup; sources show overheating is a myth, so the video says so
